title: The staircase
hook: a man building a staircase to a palace he has never seen

segments.voice: Yesterday: soul and body, and your line, set it aside. Which big question did you put down for a while? Today, a wanderer who loves big questions too, and a strange building project. Day five hundred thirty-six.

A debating hall in Savatthi, full of wandering ascetics, and loud. They're talking about kings, robbers, armies, food, gossip. Their leader, Potthapada, sees the Buddha coming in the distance and hushes them. Quiet, friends. Here comes the recluse Gotama. He likes quiet. The ninth long discourse is the long conversation that follows, about perception, the self, and how anyone could know. And in the middle of it, the Buddha describes a man at a crossroads, building a staircase. Today: the staircase.
screen: `A NOISY DEBATING HALL.` → `QUIET, HE LIKES QUIET.` → `A MAN AT A CROSSROADS, BUILDING.`

segments.voice: Some teachers of the time said that after death the self is perfectly happy. The Buddha asks them simple questions. Do you know a world that's perfectly happy? No. Have you ever experienced even a single day, or a single night, of perfect happiness? No. Do you know a path that leads there? No. Then, he says, it's like this. A man is building a staircase at a crossroads, to climb up into a palace. Someone asks him: this palace, do you know where it is? East? West? North? South? Is it tall or short? No, I don't know. So you're building a staircase to a palace you don't know and have never seen? Yes. The Pali for staircase is nissenni, and the palace is pasada. Isn't that talk, the Buddha asks, without any foundation? The point isn't that hope is foolish. It's about honesty. If you claim certainty about a destination, it's fair to ask whether anyone has seen it, including you. Then the discourse adds a quieter teaching. Near the end, a man named Citta presses on the self, and the Buddha says the ways we name a self are like milk, curd and butter. When it's milk, nobody calls it curd. When it's curd, nobody calls it butter. These are the world's ordinary names, and the Buddha says he uses them, but without being taken in by them. So the staircase cuts two ways. Don't build toward something no one has seen. And don't mistake the names on each step for something fixed. Build where you can see where you're going: in experience you can test, one step at a time.
screen: `A PERFECTLY HAPPY SELF?` · `HAVE YOU SEEN EVEN ONE HAPPY DAY?` · `A STAIRCASE TO AN UNSEEN PALACE` · `MILK, CURD, BUTTER: JUST NAMES` · then, large: `A STAIRCASE TO WHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one assumption. Pick one thing you're working toward. A promotion, a move, a version of yourself. Picture the staircase you're building. Now ask the man's questions. Where exactly is the palace? Have I ever seen it, or tasted even a day of it? What do I actually know about it? You don't have to stop building. Just see what's real under the steps. The bell holds the time.
The staircase. A man building steps toward a palace he's never seen: claims without foundation, and names mistaken for things. Today's word.
Your line: a staircase to where. Today, when you're sure about where something leads, ask once what you've actually seen of it. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers encourage students to test teachings in their own experience rather than accept claims about unseen states, and they speak of 'conventional' language as useful without being taken as ultimate.

pairs: the wanderer who hushed the hall

myth: the teachers in DN 9 had experienced the perfect happiness they promised
asked if they'd known even one perfectly happy day or night, they say no.
Potthapada hushed his friends because the Buddha likes quiet
the hall was loud with talk of kings, robbers and gossip.

he uses the world's names, like milk, curd and butter, without being taken in by them.

fork.setup: you meet a man building a staircase at a crossroads to climb into a palace. you ask where the palace is. what does he say?
fork.reveal: he doesn't know which direction, or how tall. the Buddha uses him for any claim about a destination no one has seen.

original.note: Pali nissenni: staircase, ladder. built toward a pasada, a palace, that no one has seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: the staircase mocks people who hope for heaven.
what it means: it asks for honesty about what you've actually seen before claiming certainty.
what a scholar hears: the staircase simile appears in DN 9 and again in DN 13; the milk-curd-butter passage is a key early text for 'conventional' language (lokasamañña) used without grasping.

notes: DN 9 paraphrased. Confirm the opening (the debating hall at Savatthi, Potthapada hushing the wanderers), the 'wholly happy self after death' view and the questions put to its holders, the staircase simile (also in DN 13), and the milk / curd / butter passage.
Confirm the Pali nissenni (staircase / ladder) and pasada (palace / mansion) in this passage.
The 'most beautiful woman' simile that accompanies the staircase is left out here; it may be used on day 541.
Editor review: the milk/curd/butter simile is addressed to Citta Hatthisariputta near the end of DN 9, not to Potthapada; fixed the attribution.
